analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice lawsuits at $250,000 and shields FDA-approved drugs from punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 229-197 on May 12, 2004, then laid it on the table the same day, so the Senate never voted and it never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for medical malpractice lawsuits nationwide. It would cap compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, make punitive damages nearly impossible to win, bar punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products were approved by the FDA, and limit the percentage lawyers can charge injured patients. Supporters argued this would lower malpractice insurance premiums and health care costs; the people who lose out are patients hurt by medical errors, who would collect less and have a harder time finding a lawyer.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, malpractice insurers, and drug and device manufacturers would pay out less when patients are harmed. Health care providers would face fewer lawsuits, smaller verdicts, and predictable damages, and insurers would face capped exposure. Supporters argued the savings would trickle to patients through lower malpractice premiums and less costly "defensive medicine," though the bill's text enforces the savings on the defendant side, not the patient side.

how_it_helps.text: The bill keeps unlimited recovery of economic damages — medical bills, lost earnings, and other out-of-pocket losses — while capping only noneconomic damages like pain and suffering at $250,000.
Each defendant would pay only its own proportional share of fault, ending the practice of one "deep pocket" defendant covering the share of parties unable to pay.
The bill includes a non-binding statement that a health insurer should be liable for harm caused when it decides what care is medically necessary.
Supporters' stated purpose was to lower malpractice insurance costs, reduce defensive medicine, and improve patient access to care by reducing the liability burden on the health care system.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical errors would bear the cost. Pain-and-suffering awards would be capped at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury — a figure that falls hardest on children, retirees, and people without high earnings, whose economic damages are small. Punitive damages would require proof of malicious intent or deliberate disregard by clear and convincing evidence, and juries would never be told these caps exist. Fee caps on contingency lawyers and a one-to-three-year filing deadline would make some cases too expensive to bring.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies regardless of how catastrophic the injury is, and the jury deciding the case is never informed that the cap exists — so jurors may award what they think is fair only to have a judge cut it later.

Drug and device makers whose products won FDA approval would be immune from punitive damages, and doctors who prescribe or dispense such products could not even be named in a product liability lawsuit — with narrow exceptions such as knowingly hiding information from the FDA or bribing an FDA official.

Contingent fees would be capped in tiers — 40 percent of the first $50,000, falling to 15 percent of anything over $600,000 — which plaintiff lawyers argue would make smaller malpractice cases uneconomical to take, leaving injured patients with no practical way to sue.

Punitive damages would require proving by clear and convincing evidence that the provider acted with malicious intent to injure or deliberately failed to avoid injury it knew was substantially certain — a standard far beyond ordinary negligence, so even reckless but non-malicious misconduct would escape punishment.

The bill preempts state law, overriding state rules that give injured patients more time to file, larger damages, or protection against subrogation liens — though it leaves in place state caps that are tighter and protections for providers that are stronger than its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but diffuse and unproven: lower malpractice premiums and less defensive medicine were the argument, but nothing in the record verifies that patients would see the savings. The costs are concrete and fall on a small group — patients seriously hurt by negligence, especially those with low earnings whose main loss is pain and suffering, and people harmed by FDA-approved drugs, who would lose punitive remedies almost entirely. The fee caps, which on their face look like patient protection, also function to shrink the pool of lawyers willing to take meritorious cases. The strongest version of this reform would pair damage limits with guaranteed savings passed to patients; this bill does not.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 229-197, but under the rule written for the debate the passed bill was laid on the table rather than sent to the Senate, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced May 5, 2004 by Rep. James Greenwood and referred to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees.
It had 23 cosponsors, 21 Republicans and 2 Democrats.
The Rules Committee adopted a rule that allowed only one hour of debate, closed the bill to amendments, and provided that after passage it would be laid on the table.
Rep. John Conyers moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add a complete new text; the motion failed 193-231, with 189 of 205 Democrats voting yes and only 3 of 227 Republicans.
The bill passed 229-197, with 214 of 227 Republicans voting yes and 15 of 205 Democrats.

The same day, the House agreed without objection to lay the passed bill on the table, which prevented it from being sent to the Senate; no Senate action ever occurred and the 108th Congress ended January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients and their lawyers are better off because the bill died — patients keep current malpractice rights and larger recoveries. Had it passed, malpractice insurers, health care providers, and drug and device manufacturers would have been the gainers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients, who kept full malpractice rights

for.name: Rep. James C. Greenwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with Reps. Cox and Barton as original cosponsors.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the rule (H. Res. 638) that gave the bill one hour of debate, barred amendments, and laid the passed bill on the table.

against.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to substitute a complete new text; the motion failed 193-231.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split sharply by party: 214 of 227 Republicans voted for passage while 15 of 205 Democrats did, and on the earlier motion to recommit the numbers flipped — 189 of 205 Democrats yes, 3 of 227 Republicans yes.

industries.note: Damage caps, a near-ban on punitive damages, and shortened filing deadlines directly reduce what insurers must pay on claims. The savings accrue to the insurers and the providers they cover, not to the injured patient whose award is cut.

Providers would face fewer lawsuits, predictable damage limits, and no liability for other parties' shares of a judgment. Supporters argued patients would benefit through lower premiums and less defensive medicine, but the bill's text enforces nothing on that side.

A maker of an FDA-approved drug or device would be immune from punitive damages except where it knowingly misled the FDA or bribed an official, and the prescribing doctor could not be sued in a product suit. This converts FDA approval into a litigation shield even when the agency's approval process is later shown to have been flawed.

Tiered caps on contingency fees and a shorter filing window would cut lawyer revenue on malpractice cases and likely shrink the number of cases taken. Because injured patients typically pay lawyers only out of winnings, this also reduces patients' practical access to the courts.
